🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.85% (intraday, 7-year +12bp). At trading day 6 (last close) it was -1.22% against a five-campaign average of -0.15% at the same point — only 2022-23 was worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +14bp since the hike vs a +1bp campaign average at the same point.
  • Stocks: Stocks rose everywhere; the Dow led and small caps barely moved.
  • FX: The dollar eased a little; the euro stays in its downtrend.
  • Technicals: The S&P and Nasdaq are far above their averages. The 10-year yield is stretched too.
  • Sectors: Tech leads by a wide margin. Utilities, real estate and materials lagged all month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Companies pay close to their lowest borrowing premiums on record, so there's little cushion.
  • Crisis: Systemic stress is moderate. Government debt costs are the main pressure point.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is cooling, but energy keeps about half the price basket running hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip stocks and credit markets look like 2000. Overall valuations and investor sentiment don't.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron's report is next week's big test. Oura plans a roughly $2B stock debut.
  • Iran: Iran offered a seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz. Oil fell on the news.
  • Warsh: Warsh sees inflation as too high and gives no rate guidance.
  • Week Ahead: Next week brings the jobs report, the factory survey, and Micron and Accenture earnings.
  • Outlook: The short-term bias is cautiously positive. Rising long-term yields are the main risk.
  • Trades: Buy the 10-year Treasury tactically, trim junk bonds, and keep chip exposure light.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 24 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +1.14 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 99th pctile, +4bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: The rally holds, but prices leave little room for bad news.

Friday closed higher across the board. The S&P 500 rose 0.51% to 7743.41, the Nasdaq Composite 0.48% to 27068.72 and the Dow 0.93% to 51828.62, while the Russell 2000 was nearly flat (+0.07%). The VIX fell 5.1% to 14.87. The biggest story was energy and geopolitics. Iran's foreign minister said mediators had sent the White House a seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, built on the June memorandum of understanding (Khaleej Times, CBS). Brent fell 2.14% to 104.32 and WTI fell 2.33% to 92.41. Treasuries twisted: the 2-year yield fell 7.3bp to 4.8516% and the 10-year fell 3.7bp to 5.1604%, but the 30-year rose 1.5bp to 5.4905%. The curve steepened from the front end while the long bond kept its term-premium bid. Credit did not join the relief. US HY OAS showed +8bp on the day and EM USD OAS widened 8bp to 1.64%, though both remain near historic tights. Sentiment is constructive but complacent. Equities are at 100th-percentile stretch versus history (computed), volatility is low, and the market heads into a data-heavy week with a hawkish Fed chair.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Growth leadership is intact and narrowing. In the US, Info Tech is +0.99% 1d, +3.11% 1w, +7.30% 1m and +28.28% YTD, and Comm Services is +4.77% 1m. Nearly every other sector is negative over the month: Utilities -8.77%, Real Estate -7.19%, Materials -6.69%, Financials -5.64%, Industrials -5.32%, Cons Discr -4.64%, Cons Staples -3.01%, Health Care -1.37%. Energy is a small positive at +0.16%. The rate-sensitive defensives (Utilities, Real Estate) are being punished by a 5%+ 10Y, so this is not a classic defensive rotation. Money is crowding into tech. Energy is +35.56% YTD but -2.99% on the week, down 0.87% on Friday as crude fell. Globally the pattern matches: Info Tech is +35.63% YTD and +3.77% 1m, while Materials -7.36%, Real Estate -6.77% and Utilities -5.65% lag over the month. Cons Discr is -8.16% YTD globally, a warning on the consumer. Net: growth over value, and tech over both cyclicals and defensives. That narrow concentration raises fragility.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.14 vol points (96th percentile of the 27 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 96.0 (69th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 37bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.20%2026-09-24

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (100bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.20 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
11 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 62/100
Partially 2000-like, not a full replica. Among the Equity Froth indicators, broad valuation is far from the peak: Nasdaq trailing P/E is 39.01x versus 175x, only 15% of the way to 2000 conditions, and the Nasdaq's stretch over its 200DMA is at 20%. Semis are the exception: SOX P/E of 57.74x is 94% of the way to the 2000 peak. Late-cycle catalysts are mixed. Credit tightness already exceeds 2000 conditions (IG 135%, Baa-10Y 182%) and the curve reads 69%, but the ISM PMIs have not rolled over (8% and 6%), and that rollover is the missing trigger. The macro regime reads capital crowded into equities (commodities vs equities 200%), though the dollar is only at 37%. Among the signposts, complacency is extreme (VIX 200%, NFCI 163%) but retail euphoria is absent (AAII 11%, confidence 27%). Bottom line: a pocket of mania in semis and credit, but not a market-wide March-2000 top.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The five inputs here are analyst estimates, not Bloomberg data: S&P 500 top-10 weight ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth ~60/100 and long-term EPS-growth expectations ~70/100. The IPO estimate reflects IPO-calendar reporting that 2026 proceeds are up nearly 400% even as deal counts fell about 30%, so froth is concentrated in a few giant deals rather than a 1999-style flood of small listings. The computed indicators say the market lacks two classic ingredients of 2000: a sentiment blow-off (AAII bull-bear -15.4) and a manufacturing rollover (ISM Mfg 54.6, Services 55.4). Where it resembles 2000 is extreme conditions in the leadership group (semis) and in credit and volatility pricing. That makes Micron's September 30 report, with consensus EPS of about $31.56 against $3.03 a year ago, a real-time test of whether leadership earnings can justify semis valuations. The historical template is the 2000–02 drawdown, a 78.0% fall over 31 months (computed). Warning signs to watch: a PMI rollover, rising SLOOS tightening and a semis earnings disappointment happening together.

Sources: Renaissance Capital – 2026 Recently Priced IPOs · Benzinga – Micron Earnings Preview: $31 Per Share Vs $3 A Year Ago

⚔️Iran War

On Sept 25, Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi said mediators had given the White House a new seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks to end the war. The proposal builds on the memorandum of understanding Iran and the US signed in June (Khaleej Times; CBS News). Tehran says it hopes Washington returns to the MoU before the US midterms (Al Jazeera, Sept 24). The talks in New York have moved into a technical phase, with experts joining after a first meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. President Pezeshkian said Iran was 'open' to inspections of its nuclear facilities (Just Security, Sept 25). In Washington, the Senate narrowly rejected a war-powers resolution requiring congressional authorization; the House passed a separate withdrawal resolution the previous week (Just Security). The war began Feb 28, 2026 and has cost the US an estimated $43.6B (Just Security/Britannica). Market read (analyst): Friday's 2.1–2.3% crude drop fits these de-escalation headlines, but Hormuz is not yet reopened.

Sources: Khaleej Times – Iran sends latest proposal to US to end war, reopen Hormuz within a week (Sept 25, 2026) · CBS News – Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz · Just Security – Early Edition: September 25, 2026 · Al Jazeera – Tehran says hopes US returns to MoU before elections (Sept 24, 2026) · Britannica – 2026 Iran war

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next FOMC (date not verified here): hold at a restrictive setting, with a hawkish bias and a live option to hike again (inference). Warsh warned at Jackson Hole that inflation is still too high and the Fed may have 'work to do'. He also said financial conditions are not restrictive, and Friday's loose NFCI (-0.56) and tight spreads support that view. He refuses to give forward guidance, so every meeting is live.

~1 YEAR

Over roughly 12 months (inference): policy stays restrictive, with short-term rates as the main instrument. The balance sheet keeps shortening in average duration rather than being used as a stimulus tool. Easing is unlikely unless financial conditions tighten materially, for example spreads widening or equities correcting. This may put the Fed at odds with Treasury.

On the record: at Jackson Hole (Aug 28) Warsh signaled stubborn inflation may require rate hikes (PBS, NPR, Washington Post). He cited 'financial conditions' repeatedly and judged them not restrictive (CNBC, Sept 25). He reiterated that short-term rates should remain the primary policy tool, which implies continued shortening of the balance sheet's duration (CNBC, Sept 25). Analysts said the speech pushed hike odds higher, with fed funds futures at 60.4% for a September hike at the time, and could put the Fed at odds with Treasury (CNBC, Aug 31). CNBC reports his 'regime change' at the Fed is pushing ahead but meeting internal resistance (Sept 25). Inference flag: the near-term and one-year paths above are my extrapolation from these statements, not announced policy. Whether the September hike was delivered was not verified in this search.
